intro: Hello! This is a K-TALIM audio lesson. Lesson one has twenty-four words: countries, jobs and the most useful question words. You will hear each word slowly in Korean first, and then learn what it means. Every time you hear a Korean word, say it out loud. Let's begin!
outro: Well done! You have heard every word of lesson one. Listen to this audio once more tomorrow, then practise on the site, and the words will stay with you. See you soon!

phrases.check: Now test yourself. I say the meaning, you remember the Korean word.
phrases.quick: Quick review. I say the meaning, you remember the Korean word.
phrases.review: Now let's go over the whole lesson. Listen to the Korean word and recall its meaning.

words.tip: Germans call their country Deutschland. The Korean name comes from the same word: doitch, dog-il.
Mi means beautiful and guk means country. So in Korean, America is the beautiful country.
Yeong comes from the word England. The final guk again means country.
Il means sun and bon means origin: the land where the sun rises.
Jung means middle. China called itself the country in the middle of the world.
Picture a kangaroo hopping: ho, ju, ho, ju. That is Australia.
Han is the name of the Korean people, guk means country. Remember: a word ending in guk is often a country.
Korean has no z sound, so it is said with a j: u, jeu, be, ki, seu, tan.
Just like Uzbekistan, it ends in seu-tan.
Gyeongchal means police and gwan means official. A police official.
Yori means cooking and sa means a professional. A cooking professional, a chef.
Ui means medicine, and sa again means a professional, the same sa as in the word for chef.
words.ex: My older sister is a doctor.

words.tip: Hak means learning. The word for school starts the same way: hakgyo.
Hoesa means company and won means member. A company member, an office worker.
words.ex: My father is an office worker.

words.tip: The ending nim shows respect. Teachers are always spoken to with respect.
This word always comes before a noun, as in which country.
You need this word to ask someone what they do.
Use it when you talk to older people or to people you don't know.
Ireum means name. It is the first question when you meet someone.
Use it to ask about a person.
It points to something near you and comes before a noun: this person, this book.
It is often used with the word for this: this thing.
This short form is what people say in daily conversation.
This is the full, formal form of the previous word. You will find it in books and formal speech.
